method: Researched and written with web-search verification, revised twice (current vendor documentation; evidence-grade audit); then fact-checked independently by a second agent, which read every decoded string in ch1.json and every <text> label in ch1-fig-1..4.svg. On October 12, 2026 it fetched the live Anthropic pages (Prompting best practices through WebFetch; Best practices for Claude Code, Define success criteria and Structured outputs as .md files through curl) and compared every Anthropic quotation and paraphrase word for word. The OpenAI GPT-5.5 guide, the Runway Gen-4 guide and the Google Imagen guide could not be reached (DNS failure, then proxy CONNECT 403), so their wording was confirmed through web-search excerpts of the vendor pages. AmbiEnt (1,645 examples, 32% vs 90%, pp. 790–807), Min et al. (12 models, pp. 11048–11064, DOI) and the Mars Climate Orbiter board's root and contributing causes were confirmed by web search. A search for later formatting-sensitivity work turned up He et al. (2024). ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3, the Scrum Guide 2020, Gherkin keywords, the Cucumber Book (2nd ed., 2017), Sclar et al. (ICLR 2024) and Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. (CHI 2023) were checked from expert knowledge. Formal terms (constraint, non-functional requirement, definition of done, Gherkin, zero/one/few-shot, JSON Schema, acceptance criterion) were compared against standard usage. Each of the 11 Prompt kit templates was tested against the chapter's own advice and the live vendor docs. All 16 multiple-choice keys, both sort exercises (20 items) and the order exercise were solved blind before the keys were compared.

corrections.quote: What failed was the check: nothing in the process compared the delivered file against the spec before it was trusted.
corrections.correction: The investigation board named the unit error as the root cause and listed several contributing causes, among them the lack of complete end-to-end verification of the navigation software, so the gap that matters here was a missing check.
corrections.why: The Phase I report (NASA release of November 10, 1999) names the metric-unit error in the “Small Forces” file as the root cause and lists several contributing causes, including inadequate consideration of the mission as a total system, inconsistent communication and training within the project, a navigation team not fully familiar with the spacecraft, and incomplete end-to-end verification. “What failed was the check” presents one contributing cause as the whole explanation, and “nothing in the process” overstates the board's finding. Section 1.2 reading[1] words this more carefully (“Among the contributing causes”).

corrections.quote: Every firing’s effect was underestimated by a factor of 4.45
corrections.correction: The effect of the small thruster firings recorded in that file was underestimated by a factor of 4.45
corrections.why: The “Small Forces” file held impulse data for the small thruster firings (angular momentum desaturation events and similar). It did not cover every engine firing, such as the trajectory correction maneuvers, which were modeled separately. Section 1.2 reading[1] correctly says “thruster firings” without “every”.

corrections.quote: It failed because nothing checked the delivered file against it
corrections.correction: It failed in part because no step verified the delivered file against it
corrections.why: The sentence before this one correctly says the missing end-to-end verification was among the contributing causes. This sentence then makes it the only cause, which the board did not find (see the hook correction).

corrections.where: 1.2 reading[5], which models the CRITICAL/MUST note covers
corrections.quote: some recent Claude models (it names Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6) are more responsive to the system prompt than earlier ones
corrections.correction: two Claude models (it names Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6, both since superseded) are more responsive to the system prompt than the models before them
corrections.why: The live page, fetched October 12, 2026, says: “Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 are also more responsive to the system prompt than previous models.” The quote is accurate, but the page's list of current models now runs to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1. Calling 4.5 and 4.6 “recent” in October 2026 misdates the advice. The same wording (“recent models”) appears in the 1.2 misconception fact and on slide 6, and should be changed to match.

corrections.quote: What happens with current Claude models as of October 2026, and what should you use instead?
corrections.correction: What happens with Claude 4.6 and later models as of October 2026, and what should you use instead?
corrections.why: The live guide says prefill on the last assistant turn is unsupported “starting with Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview” and that “Earlier models continue to support prefills.” Claude Haiku 4.5 is still on the page's list of current models, so “current Claude models” overstates the scope. The key (choice 3) stays correct once the stem is scoped. Slide 9's notes (“no longer work on current Claude models”) need the same fix.

corrections.where: 1.4 reading[5], Sclar caveat on newer models
corrections.quote: newer models may be less sensitive, which nobody has shown in the same way
corrections.correction: later work suggests larger, newer models are less sensitive but not immune (He and colleagues, 2024, found GPT-4 more robust to prompt templates than GPT-3.5, though results still varied by format)
corrections.why: This is a universal negative about the literature that cannot be verified, and it is close to contradicted. He et al. (2024, arXiv:2411.10541, “Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?”) varied prompt templates and found GPT-4 more robust than GPT-3.5 (up to 40% variation for GPT-3.5 on one task), with no format best across the board. If no new citation is wanted, write “how much less sensitive newer models are is not settled”.

corrections.quote: the Scrum framework’s term for the checklist that applies to every piece of work, while acceptance criteria belong to one item
corrections.correction: the Scrum Guide’s term for the formal description of the quality every increment must meet, which teams usually keep as a checklist that applies to every piece of work, while acceptance criteria belong to one item
corrections.why: The Scrum Guide (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020) defines it as “a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product”. “Checklist” is common practitioner shorthand, not the Guide's wording, and “acceptance criteria” is not a Scrum Guide term. The sentence also has no citation, although the plan's reference shelf lists the 2020 Scrum Guide for exactly this, so it should be added to 1.3's sources.

corrections.quote: Current models follow your words precisely, so say the action you want and describe what should be present.
corrections.correction: Anthropic’s guide (October 2026) says its current models follow instructions precisely, so say the action you want and describe what should be present.
corrections.why: This is vendor guidance (1.1 reading[2] attributes it to Anthropic), but here it is stated as an undated fact about all models. That breaks the book's own convention (b).

corrections.quote: models fill unmade decisions with defaults, often pick one reading of ambiguous words without saying so, follow wording precisely and, in some media, handle prohibitions badly
corrections.correction: models fill unmade decisions with defaults, often (practitioners report) pick one reading of ambiguous words without saying so, follow wording precisely (Anthropic’s guidance for its models) and, in some media, handle prohibitions badly (as at least one video vendor documents)
corrections.why: In the body, “picks one reading” is marked as practitioner report, “precise instruction following” is Anthropic's claim about Claude, and the negation problem is Runway's documentation about Gen-4. The overview presents all three as plain facts about models in general, in the same paragraph that promises every claim is marked.

corrections.where: 1.1 misconception fact, opinion stated as fact
corrections.quote: Capability helps a model carry out a request, not recover the parts you left out.
corrections.correction: In my experience, capability helps a model carry out a request far more than it helps it recover the parts you left out.
corrections.why: No cited source supports this. More capable models do infer some unstated intent from context, and vendors describe exactly that, for example Anthropic's guidance on inferring “above and beyond” behavior only when asked. As a flat statement it is opinion, so it needs a marker under convention (c).

corrections.quote: Testers in every field learn the same lesson: criteria chosen after seeing a result make it too easy to accept whatever came back.
corrections.correction: Testers and experimenters learn the same lesson, which is why scientists preregister their criteria: criteria chosen after seeing a result make it too easy to accept whatever came back.
corrections.why: “In every field” is an uncited universal claim. The idea is sound and has an established basis (preregistration, guarding against confirmation bias), so either cite that or mark the sentence as practice.

corrections.where: 1.4 reading[5], “another draw from the same request”
corrections.quote: so you are mostly asking for another draw from the same request
corrections.correction: so, in my experience, the model has little more to go on than before
corrections.why: In a continuing chat the model also sees its failed attempt and your objection, so the request is not literally “the same request”. That differs from regenerating, which the 1.4 misconception fact covers correctly. The sentence is the author's inference stated as fact, and it does not match how chat context works.

summary: Every Anthropic quotation (brilliant new employee, golden rule, can-you-suggest, ellipses, examples and 3–5 tags, smoothly flowing prose, prefill 400 from Claude 4.6, CRITICAL/MUST, Claude Code check, evidence, interview, more-than-twice and clean-session lines, F1 0.85) matches the live pages of October 12, 2026; the OpenAI, Runway, Imagen, AmbiEnt, Min and MCO details are confirmed; all 37 keys agree, and the earlier check's ten fixes are all in place. The remaining problems are classification and scope: the hook and 1.2 reduce the Orbiter's several contributing causes to one missing check; the prefill and CRITICAL/MUST notes are scoped to “current” or “recent” models although the October 2026 page lists newer models and Haiku 4.5 still accepts prefill; one universal negative about newer models is contradicted by later work; and a few vendor claims, opinions and the Scrum definition of done appear unattributed, unmarked or uncited.
